text: The dodo was a big, [[@penguin-flight|flightless bird]] that lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. It was a kind of giant pigeon, about 1 m tall. Sailors first saw it in 1598. By the end of the 1600s, it was gone.

People did hunt dodos, but the bigger problem was what they brought with them. [[@invasive-species|Pigs, rats, monkeys and dogs]] ate dodo eggs and chicks, and settlers cut down the forests. A bird that nested on the ground and had never met a [[predator|predator]] could not cope.

A turkey
An ostrich

st.reveal: DNA from dodo bones shows it was a giant, flightless pigeon. Its closest living relative is the colourful Nicobar pigeon, found on islands in the Bay of Bengal, including India's Nicobar Islands.

myth: The dodo died out because it was fat, slow and stupid.

The dodo was well suited to its island, which had no ground predators. It had no reason to fear people or animals. It died out because humans and the animals they brought arrived suddenly, not because it was foolish.
facts: Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean

sec.t:
Mauritius lies about 2,000 km off the coast of Africa, far from any big land. Before people arrived, there were no ground-dwelling [[mammal|mammals]] that hunted birds. The dodo's ancestors were pigeons that flew there long ago.

With plenty of fallen fruit and no predators, flying became unnecessary. Over many generations, the birds grew larger and their wings shrank. This happens again and again on [[@islands-world|islands]]. [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]] had [[@lost-moa|giant flightless moas]], and [[@madagascar|Madagascar]] had elephant birds.

sec.h: A dodo in a Mughal painting
sec.t:
A few live dodos were taken away by ship. At least one seems to have reached India. Around 1625, the Mughal court artist Ustad Mansur, famous for his pictures of animals, painted a dodo among other birds for the emperor Jahangir. The painting shows grey feathers, a big hooked beak and yellow legs.

Scientists value it as one of the most realistic pictures of a living dodo. Many European paintings show fat, comical birds. Some of those may have been overfed captives, or copies of copies. [[@mughal-miniatures|Mughal painters]] worked from life.

For a long time, almost nothing remained. The Oxford University Museum of Natural History has the only dodo with surviving soft tissue: a dried head and a foot. In 1865, a schoolteacher on Mauritius found hundreds of dodo bones in a marsh called the Mare aux Songes. Most dodo skeletons in museums today are built from those marsh bones.

[[dna|DNA]] from dodo bones confirmed in 2002 that it was a pigeon. Its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, a shimmering green bird found on islands in the Bay of Bengal, including India's Nicobar Islands. The dodo was a pigeon and therefore, like all [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]], a kind of dinosaur.

In 1865, the same year as the marsh discovery, Lewis Carroll put a Dodo in [[@alice-wonderland|Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]]. His real name was Charles Dodgson, and some people think he chose the bird as a joke about his own name. The book made the dodo famous.

Today the dodo appears on the coat of arms of Mauritius. The phrase "dead as a dodo" became a way of saying something is gone for good. It is also a warning that [[@extinction-today|extinctions are still happening]].

text: Satellites are machines that circle Earth, high above the air. More than 10,000 of them are working right now. They do four big jobs. Weather satellites watch clouds, storms and oceans. Communication satellites carry TV, radio and some phone and internet signals. [[navigation|Navigation]] satellites, like [[@gps-how|GPS]], help phones, ships and planes work out where they are. And Earth-watching satellites photograph forests, farms, cities and ice.
You may not notice them, but you probably used a satellite today. If you checked the weather, followed a map, watched live sport or paid by card, a satellite was likely somewhere in the chain.

st.reveal: At about 36,000 km above the equator, a satellite takes exactly one day to go round Earth. Since Earth also turns once a day, the satellite seems to hang still in the sky, so dishes can point at one fixed spot.

d.try: With an adult, look up today's satellite cloud picture on the India Meteorological Department website or NOAA's website. Then go outside and look at the sky. Do it every day for a week and see whether the clouds you notice match what the satellite shows over your area.
myth: When you use the internet or make a phone call, the signal usually goes through a satellite.

Most calls and internet traffic travel through mobile towers and cables, including huge cables on the sea floor that carry the vast majority of data between continents. Satellites help in remote places, on ships and planes, and in disasters.

sec.t:
Before satellites, forecasters could only see weather where there were people to report it. Huge storms could form over the ocean unseen. In 1960 the US launched TIROS-1, the first weather satellite, and its first fuzzy picture of clouds changed forecasting for good.

Today India's INSAT satellites and America's GOES satellites send fresh images every 15 minutes or less. They help forecasters track the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] and spot [[@cyclones-india|cyclones]] days before they reach land.

{{story:weather-forecasts}}

In October 2013, Cyclone Phailin, one of the strongest storms to hit India in years, struck [[@odisha|Odisha]]. Thanks to satellite tracking and good forecasts, authorities moved close to a million people to safety, and far fewer lives were lost than in a similar [[cyclone|cyclone]] in 1999.

In 1945, the science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke pointed out something useful. A satellite about 36,000 km above the [[equator|equator]] takes exactly one day to circle Earth. Because Earth turns at the same rate, the satellite seems to stay in one spot.

This is called a geostationary [[orbit|orbit]]. It is why the TV dish on a roof can point at one place and never move. Communication and weather satellites often sit there, each able to see a huge part of the globe at once.

Most other satellites fly much lower, a few hundred to a few thousand kilometres up, and race around Earth in about 90 minutes to two hours. Lower satellites can take sharper pictures. Signals to and from them also arrive with much less delay, which is why new internet satellites fly low.

In 1975, India borrowed time on an American satellite for a year-long experiment called SITE, the Satellite Instructional [[@television-invented|Television]] Experiment. Community TV sets were placed in about 2,400 villages across six states. Every day they showed programmes on farming, health, hygiene and science, many in local languages.

For many villagers it was the first television they had ever seen. The experiment showed that satellites could reach places that cables never would, and it helped persuade India to build its own INSAT satellites. [[@satellites-india|India's satellites]] now support everything from TV to fishing.

Earth-watching satellites have photographed the planet since the US launched Landsat 1 in 1972. They show farmers how healthy crops are, help track [[@forest-fires|forest fires]] and floods, measure melting [[@glaciers|glaciers]] and [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]], and help draw accurate maps. ISRO's satellites help India estimate harvests and plan where to dig wells.

Fishing boats along India's coast get messages, based on satellite readings of sea temperature and [[plankton|plankton]], about where fish are likely to gather. That saves fuel and time.

Many satellites carry extremely precise clocks. Phone networks, power grids and banks use satellite time signals to keep their computers in step. When you tap a card to pay, a satellite clock may help stamp the exact time of the payment.

Not everything goes through space, though. Most of the world's internet traffic travels through cables, many of them on the sea floor, as you can read in [[@internet-how|how the internet works]].

text: The ocean sunfish, or mola, is one of the strangest fish in the sea. It looks like a big, flat disc, as if someone took a fish and cut off the back half. It has a tall fin on top, another underneath, and a short, frilly edge where a tail should be.

Sunfish are also giants. The heaviest bony fish ever weighed was a bump-head sunfish found floating dead near the Azores islands in the Atlantic in 2021. It weighed 2,744 kg, about as much as two cars, and was more than 3 metres long. Sunfish live in warm and mild seas around the world.

st.prompt: Ocean sunfish are often seen lying flat on their sides at the surface. Why?

options.t: To warm up after cold deep dives and let birds pick off parasites
Because they are sick or dying
To sleep where predators cannot reach

st.reveal: Sunfish hunt jellyfish in cold, deep water and then return to bask near the warm surface. While they lie there, seabirds and small fish nibble parasites from their skin.

d.try: Put a scrap of thin, clear plastic bag into a bowl of water and stir gently. Watch how it floats and ripples. To a hungry sunfish or sea turtle, it looks a lot like a jellyfish, which is why plastic in the sea is so dangerous for them.
myth: Sunfish are lazy drifters that float wherever the currents take them.
Tagging studies show sunfish swim actively, dive hundreds of metres to feed and travel long distances. Their lying-at-the-surface habit made people think they were helpless.

sec.h: A fish without a back end
sec.t:
As a baby sunfish grows, its tail never forms properly. Instead, the back edges of its top and bottom fins fold together into a stiff, wavy flap called a clavus, which it uses as a rudder.

To swim, the sunfish flaps its two tall fins from side to side, together, like a bird flapping wings sideways. It looks clumsy, but it works. Tagging studies show sunfish can cruise at a steady pace and dive hundreds of metres down.

When the top fin sticks out of the water, beach-goers sometimes panic and shout "shark". But [[@sharks-myths|sharks]] swim with their fin steady, while a sunfish's fin flops slowly from side to side.

Sunfish mainly eat [[@jellyfish-old|jellyfish]], plus comb jellies, small squid and fish. Jellyfish are about 95 per cent water and very low in food value, so a sunfish has to eat a huge amount to grow so big. Its mouth is fused into a beak, and teeth in its throat shred the slippery food before swallowing.

They hunt in cold, deep water, often down to the dim [[@ocean-zones|twilight zone]], where light barely reaches. Then they come back up.

After a cold dive, a sunfish often lies flat on its side at the surface, soaking up warmth. That habit gave it its English name. Warming up after a dive helps its muscles and brain work faster, the way you might sit in the sun after a cold swim.

While it lies there, seabirds such as gulls land and peck [[parasite|parasites]] off its skin. Sunfish can carry dozens of kinds of parasites. Small fish called wrasse also clean them in the kelp forests nearer shore. The Latin name, Mola, means millstone, after the fish's round, grey, rough shape.

Sunfish are harmless to people. Their beaky mouths are made for slurping soft food, not biting swimmers. But they are often caught by accident in fishing nets, especially in the Mediterranean and off California.

[[@ocean-plastic|Plastic]] is another danger. A floating bag looks a lot like a jellyfish. Sunfish, and sea turtles too, sometimes swallow bags, which can block their guts. The IUCN listed the ocean sunfish as Vulnerable in its 2015 assessment. And the sunfish is not the only giant that lives on soft, small food. The biggest of all the [[@ocean-giants|ocean giants]], the blue whale, feeds on shrimp-like krill no longer than your finger.

text: A submarine dives and rises by changing how heavy it is for its size. Along its sides are big [[ballast|ballast]] tanks. On the surface, the tanks are full of air, so the submarine floats like a ship. To dive, the crew opens valves and lets seawater flood into the tanks. Now the submarine is heavier than the water it pushes aside, and it sinks.

To come back up, the crew blows compressed air into the tanks. The air pushes the water out, and the submarine becomes light enough to rise. Small fins called hydroplanes, a bit like a plane's wings, tilt the submarine up or down as it moves forward. The same rule that keeps big steel ships afloat is at work here, as explained in [[@floating-ships|how ships float]].

st.prompt: A submarine wants to come back up to the surface. What does it do?

Drops heavy anchors on the sea floor

st.reveal: Blowing air into the ballast tanks forces seawater out of them. The submarine becomes lighter for its size than the water around it, so it floats upward, helped by angling its small fins like wings.

d.try: Make a bottle diver. Fill a plastic bottle to the top with water and drop in a small ketchup sachet or a pen cap with a blob of clay on it, so it just floats. Screw the lid on tightly. Squeeze the bottle and the diver sinks; let go and it rises. Squeezing pushes water into the diver, just like a submarine's tanks.
myth: Something made of heavy steel can't float.

Whether something floats depends on how much water it pushes aside, not just what it is made of. A steel hull full of air pushes aside a lot of water and floats. Fill it with water and it sinks, which is exactly the trick submarines use.

sec.t:
The hardest trick is not sinking or rising but staying at one depth. A submarine wants to be exactly as heavy as the water it pushes aside, so it neither sinks nor floats up. This is called being neutrally buoyant.

To get it right, submarines have smaller trim tanks. The crew pumps water between them, or in and out, to balance the boat. They must keep adjusting as people walk around inside, as fuel gets used up and as the water changes. Cold or salty water is slightly heavier, so the submarine floats a little higher in it. Fish do something similar with a gas-filled bag inside them called a swim bladder.

People dreamed of underwater boats for centuries. In the 1620s, a Dutch inventor named Cornelis Drebbel is said to have rowed a covered boat under the River Thames in London. In 1775, during the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]], an inventor named David Bushnell built the Turtle, a wooden, egg-shaped craft for one person, who turned [[propeller|propellers]] by hand. It tried to attach a bomb to a British warship but failed.

Modern submarines are far more powerful. Nuclear submarines can stay underwater for months, because their reactors need no air. They make fresh water from seawater, and split water to make oxygen for the crew. India's first home-built nuclear submarine, INS Arihant, joined the navy in 2016. Other Indian submarines are built at Mazagon Dock in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]].

Underwater, there are no windows to look out of and it is often dark. Submarines find their way using sonar, which works like the [[@echolocation|echolocation]] of [[@bats-fly|bats]] and dolphins. A sonar sends out a ping of sound and listens for echoes from the sea floor, ships or whales.

Most submarines also listen quietly, without pinging, because a ping could give away where they are. Their crews learn to recognise the sounds of different ships, and even of shrimps and whales. Inside, life is cramped. Crews may not see daylight for weeks, so the lights are dimmed at night to keep their [[@sleep-why|body clocks]] steady.

text: Very strong, for its size. The dragline silk that a spider uses as its safety rope and as the frame of its web is about as strong as high-grade steel of the same thickness. Because silk is about six times lighter than steel, it is far stronger weight for weight.

It is also tough. Silk can stretch a long way before it snaps, so it soaks up the energy of a flying insect smacking into the web. By some measures, it is tougher than Kevlar, the material in bulletproof vests.
All of this comes from a thread thinner than a human [[@hair-grow|hair]], made from nothing more than [[protein|protein]], the same kind of stuff as your skin and muscles.

st.prompt: Silkworms are farmed in huge numbers for their silk. Why aren't spiders?

Kept together in large numbers, they eat each other

st.reveal: Most spiders are loners and hunters. Crowd them together and they fight and eat one another, and each one makes only a little silk. That is why scientists are trying to get bacteria, yeast and even silkworms to make spider silk proteins instead.

d.try: On a misty or dewy morning, look for an orb web on a bush or fence, with an adult. Water droplets make every thread shine. Count the spokes and the turns of the spiral, but don't touch the web or the spider. If there's no dew, a very light mist from a plant sprayer held well back works too.
myth: All spiders spin webs to catch their food.

Every spider makes silk, but only about half of them build webs to trap prey. Jumping spiders, wolf spiders and many others hunt by stalking or ambushing, and use silk for safety lines, nests and egg sacs.

sec.t:
Inside a spider's belly are silk [[gland|glands]] full of liquid protein, a bit like [[@glue-sticky|runny glue]]. The spider squeezes it out through tiny nozzles at the tip of its body, called spinnerets.

As the liquid is pulled out, the long protein [[molecule|molecules]] line up side by side and lock together. In a fraction of a second, the liquid becomes a solid, flexible thread. The spider usually pulls the thread with its back legs or lets its own weight drag it out as it drops.

A garden orb-weaver can make up to seven kinds of silk from different glands. There is strong silk for the frame, stretchy silk dotted with [[@glue-sticky|glue]] for the sticky spiral, soft silk for egg sacs and wide bands for wrapping up prey.

In 2010, scientists described a spider from [[@madagascar|Madagascar]] that they named Darwin's bark spider. It strings webs right across rivers, with bridge lines up to about 25 m long, about the length of a tennis court.

Its silk is the toughest biological material ever measured, about twice as tough as other spider silks. Each morning, insects flying along the river crash into the web like cars into a net stretched across a road.

Spiders don't waste their silk. Many orb-weavers eat their old web before building a fresh one, [[@recycling|recycling]] the protein. A new web can take less than an hour to spin.

{{story:silk}}

Baby spiders can travel hundreds of kilometres without wings. A spiderling climbs to a high point, lifts its body and lets out fine threads of silk. The breeze, and even Earth's natural electric field, lifts it into the air. This is called ballooning.

In 1832, Charles Darwin was sailing off the coast of Argentina aboard HMS Beagle when thousands of tiny spiders landed on the ship's ropes. The nearest land was many kilometres away.

Spider silk is so hard to collect that very little cloth has ever been made from it. In Madagascar, two [[textile|textile]] makers, Simon Peers and Nicholas Godley, spent years gathering silk from wild golden orb-weaver spiders. Workers drew silk gently from each spider, then released it.

It took silk from over a million spiders to weave a shimmering golden shawl, shown at the American Museum of Natural History in New York in 2009, and later a cape. Silkworm [[@silk|silk]], by comparison, is farmed by the tonne.

Scientists dream of using spider silk for medical stitches, light ropes and strong fabrics. They have put spider silk [[gene|genes]] into [[bacteria|bacteria]], yeast, silkworms and even goats to make the protein. Getting the threads to spin as well as a spider's has proved much harder.

For years, spider silk did one useful job already. Its fine threads were used as crosshairs in [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] and gun sights, because few other materials were so thin and even.

text: Most cooking gas comes from deep underground, from the same places that give us crude oil. In India, the red cylinder in most kitchens holds LPG, short for liquefied petroleum gas. It is a mix of two gases, propane and butane, separated out at oil refineries and gas plants.

Some homes, especially in big cities, get piped natural gas instead. That gas is mostly methane and flows through underground pipes, a bit like water. In the United States, millions of homes cook on piped natural gas, while farms and barbecue grills often use propane tanks.

st.prompt: If LPG leaks in a kitchen, where does most of it collect?

options.t: Near the floor
Up near the ceiling
It spreads evenly everywhere

st.reveal: LPG is heavier than air, so a leak sinks and pools low down, a bit like invisible water. Piped natural gas is lighter than air and rises instead. That is why opening doors and windows quickly matters with either kind.

The letter is a quarter of the year (A is January to March) and the number is the year, showing when the cylinder is due for a safety test. Check whether yours is still in date.
myth: Cooking gas naturally smells of rotten eggs.

sec.t:
Natural gas formed over millions of years from tiny sea creatures and plants. When they died, they sank and were buried under mud and sand. Heat and pressure deep underground slowly cooked them into [[@oil-coal|oil and gas]], which got trapped in rock layers, sometimes under the seabed.

Companies drill wells to reach these pockets. Off the coast of Mumbai, the Bombay High field has supplied oil and gas since the 1970s. When the gas comes up, it is a mix. Plants separate the methane, which goes into pipelines, from heavier gases like propane and butane, which become LPG.

Pure LPG and methane have almost no smell, which would make leaks hard to notice. So suppliers add a tiny amount of a chemical called a mercaptan. Your [[@nose-smell|nose]] can pick it up even in very small amounts, which is why a leak smells like rotten eggs or cabbage.

If you ever notice that smell, don't touch a light switch, don't light anything and tell an adult straight away. Open windows and doors, and leave the room. A single spark can set off gas that has built up in the air.

sec.h: From wood smoke to a blue flame
sec.t:
Not long ago, most Indian homes cooked on firewood, coal, kerosene or dried cow dung cakes. These fuels fill a kitchen with smoke. The World Health Organization says smoke from cooking fires harms the lungs and causes millions of deaths around the world every year. Most of them are women and children, who spend the most time near the stove.

In 2016 India started the Ujjwala scheme to give free LPG connections to poorer families. By late 2025 it had given out about 10.3 crore. India now uses about 31 million tonnes of LPG a year, and more than half of it arrives by ship from countries such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United States.

Cooking gas is a [[fossil|fossil]] fuel, so burning it adds [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] to the air. Some villages make [[@biogas|biogas]] from cow dung and food waste in sealed tanks. Many city families now use [[@induction-stoves|induction stoves]] that heat pans with magnets and electricity. Solar cookers work well on sunny days. Still, for many cooks, nothing quite replaces the instant control of a blue flame under a hot tawa.

text: इकत नमूनेदार कपड़ा बनाने का एक तरीका है, जिसमें धागों को बुनने से पहले रँगा जाता है। बुनकर धागों के छोटे-छोटे गुच्छों को एक तय नमूने के हिसाब से डोरी या प्लास्टिक की पट्टियों से कसकर बाँधते हैं, फिर उन्हें रंग में डुबोते हैं। बँधे हिस्से बिना रँगे रह जाते हैं। बाँधने और रँगने के कई दौर के बाद धागों पर रंगीन टुकड़ों का एक नमूना बन जाता है। जब उन्हें [[@knitting-weaving|करघे]] पर बुना जाता है, तो वह नमूना कपड़े में उभर आता है।

यह नाम मलय और इंडोनेशियाई शब्द मेंगिकत से आया है, जिसका मतलब है बाँधना। इकत पूरे एशिया, अफ़्रीका और लैटिन अमेरिका में बनता है। भारत तीन शैलियों के लिए मशहूर है: गुजरात के पाटण का पटोला, तेलंगाना के पोचमपल्ली का इकत, और ओडिशा का संबलपुरी।

sec.h: पाटण पटोला, दोनों तरफ़ एक जैसा
sec.t:
गुजरात के पाटण का पटोला [[@silk|रेशम]] में बना दोहरा इकत है। यह दुनिया के सबसे कठिन बुने जाने वाले कपड़ों में गिना जाता है। ताना और बाना, दोनों में नमूना होने से डिज़ाइन कपड़े के दोनों तरफ़ एक जैसा साफ़ दिखता है। एक साड़ी में बुनकरों के पूरे परिवार को कई महीने लग सकते हैं।

अब बस गिने-चुने परिवार ही असली पाटण पटोला बनाते हैं। सदियों पहले पटोला कपड़ा दक्षिण-पूर्व एशिया तक बिकने जाता था, जहाँ इंडोनेशिया के राजपरिवार इसे खज़ाने की तरह सँभालते थे और स्थानीय बुनकर इसकी नकल करते थे। वहाँ रस्मों की पोशाकों पर भी पटोला के नमूने इस्तेमाल होते थे। एक पाटण पटोला साड़ी लाखों रुपये की हो सकती है, क्योंकि उसमें इतने महीनों का हुनरमंद काम लगता है।

हैदराबाद के पास गाँवों का एक समूह, पोचमपल्ली, सूती और रेशमी कपड़े में गाढ़े [[geometry|ज्यामितीय]] इकत बनाता है, अक्सर हीरे और टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी लकीरों वाले। 2005 में पोचमपल्ली इकत जीआई टैग पाने वाले भारत के शुरुआती हथकरघों में से एक बना।

ओडिशा में संबलपुरी इकत, जिसे बंधा कहते हैं, अक्सर शंख, पहिए और फूल दिखाता है। कुछ बुनकर तो जानवरों और मंदिरों की तस्वीरें भी बुन देते हैं, जिसके लिए धागा-धागा सोचकर योजना बनानी पड़ती है। 2021 में संयुक्त राष्ट्र विश्व पर्यटन संगठन ने पोचमपल्ली को दुनिया के सबसे अच्छे पर्यटन गाँवों में से एक चुना।

जापान में इकत को कसूरी कहते हैं। उज़्बेकिस्तान में बादलों जैसे नमूनों वाला चटक रेशमी इकत सिल्क रोड के अमीर व्यापारी पहनते थे। दोहरा इकत इंडोनेशिया के बाली के एक गाँव तेंगानान में भी बनता है, जहाँ गेरिंगसिंग नाम के कपड़े के बारे में माना जाता है कि वह पहनने वाले की रक्षा करता है।

आज डिज़ाइनर कपड़ों, कुशनों और स्नीकर्स तक में इकत इस्तेमाल करते हैं। और सबसे मज़े की बात? इकत का नमूना बिछाना दोहराते आकारों का जाल बनाने जैसा है, गणित की एक किस्म जिसे तुम [[@tessellations|टेसलेशन]] में खोज सकते हो।

text: A cipher is a rule for scrambling a message. Only someone who knows the rule, the key, can unscramble it.

Caesar's cipher shifts every letter by the same amount. With a shift of three, A becomes D and B becomes E. It's easy to crack today, because there are only 25 possible shifts. You could try them all before lunch.

Your phone uses much stronger codes, based on maths so hard that even powerful computers can't crack them quickly. The idea is the same as Caesar's: a rule, a key and a message that looks like nonsense to everyone else.

quiz.prompt: A message reads KHOOR. Each letter was shifted 3 places forward in the alphabet. What does it say?

options.t: HELLO

quiz.reveal: Shift each letter 3 places back. K becomes H, H becomes E, O becomes L, and R becomes O. KHOOR is HELLO.

myth: A code and a cipher are the same thing.
A code swaps whole words or ideas for other words or symbols, usually using a codebook. A cipher scrambles a message letter by letter, following a rule and a key.

sec.t:
For centuries, people swapped each letter for a different symbol, in no particular order. That gives a huge number of possible keys, far too many to try one by one. It seemed unbreakable.

Then, in the 9th century, a scholar in Baghdad named al-Kindi described a trick. In any language, some letters turn up far more often than others. In English, E is the most common, followed by T and A. So if one symbol fills a secret message, it is probably E. Count the symbols, match them to the usual letter frequencies, and the message slowly cracks open. This method, called frequency analysis, broke most secret letters for hundreds of years.

Some secret messages are codes rather than ciphers. In World War II, the US Marines used [[@navajo-nation|Navajo speakers]] who sent messages in their own language, with special words for military terms. Enemy listeners could not understand a word.

The difference matters. A cipher can be cracked by maths alone. A code, built on a language or a secret codebook, needs someone who knows the words.

Another trick is to hide that a message exists at all. This is called steganography, from Greek words meaning "covered writing". The Greek historian Herodotus told of a messenger whose head was shaved, tattooed with a secret note, and sent off once his hair had grown back.

Children have long used invisible ink made from lemon juice, which shows up brown when an adult gently warms the paper. Today, computers can hide words inside the tiny colour details of a photo, where no eye would notice. A clever spy might use both: scramble the message, then hide it.

When you see a padlock symbol in a web browser, your messages are being enciphered. Many systems rely on a neat fact about [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]]. Multiplying two huge primes together is quick. Working backwards, to find which two primes made the answer, would take ordinary computers an extremely long time.

So your phone can share a public lock that anyone may use, while keeping the key private. Underneath, every message is a long string of 1s and 0s, as explained in [[@binary-code|binary]], being scrambled by arithmetic. Caesar would recognise the idea. He would not recognise the numbers, which can run to hundreds of digits.

text: [[geometry|Geometry]] is the maths of shapes, sizes, angles and space. You use it every time you judge whether a sofa will fit through a door, cut a sandwich into triangles or aim a ball into a goal. Builders, tailors, gardeners, game designers and pilots all use it at work.

The word comes from Greek and means "earth measurement". The ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that Egyptian officials had to re-measure farmers' fields after the yearly flood of the [[@egypt-nile|Nile]] washed away the boundaries. Measuring land, buildings and the sky has driven geometry ever since.

myth: Geometry is only about drawing shapes in a maths notebook.
Geometry is used to build houses, design phones, plan roads, make maps, guide satellites and even cut cloth for clothes. Animals use it too, like bees building honeycombs.

sec.t:
Look closely at a railway bridge or a mobile phone tower and you will see triangles everywhere. A triangle is rigid. If its three sides are fixed, it cannot be squashed into a different shape. A square, in contrast, easily leans over into a diamond.

So engineers brace structures with triangles, in frames called trusses. Roofs, cranes, electricity pylons and many [[@bridges|bridges]] depend on them. Even a simple folding chair has a triangle hidden in it when it is open.

[[@circles|Circles]] have their own tricks. A manhole cover is round partly because a circle is the same width in every direction, so it cannot drop through its own hole. A square cover could be turned on its diagonal and fall in.

Bees build their [[@honeycomb|honeycombs]] from hexagons. Hexagons fit together with no gaps, like tiles on a floor, and they enclose a lot of space for the amount of wax used. In 1999, the mathematician Thomas Hales proved that hexagons are the most efficient way to divide a flat surface into equal areas.

You can find geometry in a sunflower's spirals, in the six arms of a snowflake and in the smooth curve of a thrown ball. Planets move in shapes called ellipses, a kind of stretched circle.

Spiders are geometers too. Many build orb webs with threads running out from the centre like spokes, and a spiral laid across them at fairly even spacing. Nobody teaches a young spider this. The pattern is built into its behaviour, and it gives a strong, light net that catches insects from any direction.

{{story:bridges}}

[[@maths-sport|Sport is full of geometry]]. A cricket pitch is 22 yards long, about 20.12 m, and the creases are painted at exact distances. A fielder who wants to cut off a run quickly takes the shortest path, a straight line, to where the ball will be.

In [[@carrom|carrom]], snooker and football, a ball bouncing off a wall leaves at about the same angle it arrived at. Good players learn to "see" these angles. A carrom player banking the striker off the edge to hit a coin is doing geometry by instinct.

Indian priests more than 2,500 years ago wrote down rules for building fire altars with ropes and pegs. These texts, the Sulba Sutras, include ways to make right angles and squares of a given area. The oldest, by [[@baudhayana|Baudhayana]], also states the rule now known as Pythagoras's theorem.

Today, the [[@gps-how|GPS]] in a phone works out where you are by measuring your distance from several [[@satellites-help|satellites]] at once and finding the one point that fits all those distances. Tailors, architects and video game designers rely on geometry too. A tailor turns body measurements into flat paper shapes that become a curved shirt, and a game designer builds whole worlds out of millions of tiny triangles. Even a [[@pizza|pizza]] cut into eight equal slices is a lesson in angles: each slice is 45 degrees.

text: A magic square is a grid of numbers where every row, every column and both long diagonals add up to the same total. That total is called the magic sum.
The smallest one uses the numbers 1 to 9 in a 3 by 3 grid. The top row is 8, 1, 6. The middle row is 3, 5, 7. The bottom row is 4, 9, 2.
Add any row, column or diagonal and you get 15. There is only one way to do this, if you count turned and flipped versions as the same.
Bigger magic squares exist for every size except 2 by 2. Mathematicians even have a formula for the magic sum. For a square n numbers wide, using 1 up to n × n, the sum is n × (n × n + 1) ÷ 2.

st.prompt: In a 3 by 3 magic square using the numbers 1 to 9, which number must go in the centre?
st.reveal: The numbers 1 to 9 add up to 45, so each of the three rows must add to 15. The centre square sits on four different lines, and the only number that works there is 5, the middle of 1 to 9.

myth: Magic squares are a modern puzzle invented for puzzle books.

Magic squares are well over a thousand years old. They were known in ancient China, studied by Indian and Arab mathematicians, carved into temples and painted into European art long before puzzle books existed.

sec.t:
The oldest known magic square comes from China. It is called the Lo Shu, or "scroll of the river Lo". According to legend, long ago a great flood struck China. As people made offerings to the river, a turtle crawled out with a strange pattern of dots on its shell. The dots formed the 3 by 3 square above.

The Lo Shu became important in Chinese traditions about harmony and the arrangement of homes. Nobody knows exactly how old it is, but it appears in Chinese writings from about 2,000 years ago.

sec.h: Squares in Indian temples and books
sec.t:
At [[@khajuraho|Khajuraho]] in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], the Parshvanatha temple, a Jain temple built in the 10th century, has a 4 by 4 square carved into its stone. Its magic sum is 34.

It's special even among magic squares. Besides the rows, columns and diagonals, many other groups of four add up to 34. They include the four corners, each 2 by 2 corner block and the "broken" diagonals that wrap around the edges. Squares like this are sometimes called "most perfect".

In 1356, the Indian mathematician Narayana Pandita wrote a book called *Ganita Kaumudi* with a long section explaining how to build magic squares of many sizes. Magic squares also turn up in other Indian [[@architecture-temples|temples]], on charms and in old [[manuscript|manuscripts]].

{{story:architecture-temples}}

sec.h: A square in a famous engraving
sec.t:
In 1514, the German artist Albrecht Dürer made an engraving called *Melencolia I*. It shows a gloomy winged figure surrounded by tools and puzzles. On the wall behind is a 4 by 4 magic square with a sum of 34.

Look at the bottom row and you'll find the numbers 15 and 14 side by side, making 1514, the year Dürer made the picture. Copies of the engraving are kept in [[@museums|museums]] around the world.

The American printer, scientist and statesman [[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] loved magic squares. In a letter, he admitted that as a young clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, he made them to pass the time when debates grew boring.

He built an 8 by 8 square with extra tricks. Half of each row adds up to half the magic sum, and bent rows shaped like a V also add up to the total. It is still known as Franklin's square.

Magic squares are cousins of other number grids. In a Latin square, each symbol appears once in every row and column, which is the idea behind [[@sudoku|Sudoku]]. Magic squares go further by making the numbers add up.

Today, mathematicians study them as puzzles about patterns and counting. Nobody yet knows exactly how many different 6 by 6 magic squares exist, though computers have estimated the number. For the 5 by 5 size, there are 275,305,224, found by computer in 1973.

text: Maths turns up in almost every sport. Scorers keep [[@maths-sports-stats|statistics]], coaches study data to plan tactics, engineers use physics to design better bats, balls and shoes, and broadcasters use [[geometry|geometry]] to track the ball. Even setting a fair target in a rain-hit cricket match needs a formula.

Some of the maths is simple, like adding runs or timing a race. Some is complicated, like the computer models that predict where a cricket ball would have gone if it hadn't hit the batter's pad. Either way, numbers help players train smarter, help fans understand the game, and help referees and umpires make fairer decisions.

st.reveal: Multiply the points by the chance of scoring. A two-pointer gives 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 points per try. A three-pointer gives 3 × 0.35 = 1.05. The difference looks tiny, but over a season it adds up, which is why teams now shoot many more threes.

sec.t:
In a one-day cricket match, rain can wipe out overs halfway through. How do you set a fair target for the team batting second? Simply scaling down by overs is unfair, because a team with ten wickets in hand can bat much more boldly than a team with two.

In 1997, two English statisticians, [[@maths-cricket-dls|Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis]], created a method that counts both overs and wickets as "resources". The fewer resources a team has, the lower its target. In 2014, an Australian statistician, Steven Stern, updated it for modern high-scoring games, and it became the Duckworth–Lewis–Stern, or DLS, method. Players often joke about not understanding it, but it is used in every rain-affected international one-day and T20 match.

When [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] won India's javelin gold at the [[@olympics-host|Tokyo Olympics]], his best throw flew 87.58 m. A throw like that is a lesson in angles and speed. In a world without air, the best angle to launch a thrown object is 45 degrees. Real javelins are affected by air pushing on them, and top throwers usually release at a lower angle, often around 35 degrees.

The same thinking applies to a long jumper's take-off, a footballer's free kick curling around a wall, and a spin bowler's flight. Coaches film athletes with high-speed [[@cameras-how|cameras]] and use software to measure angles and speeds, then suggest tiny changes.

Ball-tracking systems such as Hawk-Eye use several cameras around the ground. Each camera records the ball's position many times a second. A computer combines the views to work out exactly where the ball was in three dimensions, then predicts its path. In cricket, that prediction helps decide leg-before-wicket appeals. In [[@tennis|tennis]], it shows whether a ball landed in or out.

These systems are very accurate but not perfect. That is why cricket's review system has an "umpire's call" zone: if the predicted path only clips the stumps, the umpire's original decision stands. It is maths admitting its own margin of error, which good [[@statistics-lies|statistics]] always should.

text: Probability is the maths of how likely something is. It gives every possible event a number between 0 and 1. Zero means it can never happen. One means it is certain. A half means it is as likely to happen as not.

For simple cases, you count. A dice has six faces, and one of them shows a six. So the chance of rolling a six is 1 in 6. A [[@cards-games|pack of cards]] has 52 cards, and 4 of them are aces, so the chance of drawing an ace is 4 in 52, or 1 in 13.
Probability can't tell you what will happen next. It tells you what will happen over and over again, in the long run.

More than half, because it's on a streak

st.reveal: A coin has no memory. Each flip is a fresh start with a 1 in 2 chance of heads. Believing that tails is "due" is such a common mistake that it has a name, the gambler's fallacy.

sec.t:
Probability began with a gambling puzzle. In 1654, a French gambler asked the mathematician Blaise Pascal how to fairly split the money if [[@maths-games|a game of dice]] was stopped halfway. Pascal wrote letters about it to another mathematician, Pierre de Fermat.

Between them, they worked out a way to count every possible way the game could have finished, and share the money according to each player's chances. Their letters laid the foundations of probability. Today the same ideas are used by weather forecasters, doctors, [[@insurance|insurance companies]] and scientists.

Most people guess that you'd need around 180 people in a room before two of them probably [[@puzzle-birthday|share a birthday]], about half of 365. The real answer is just 23.

The trick is that you aren't looking for someone who shares *your* birthday. Any two people will do. With 23 people there are 253 different pairs, and each pair is a small chance of a match. All those small chances add up quickly. With 70 people, a shared birthday is almost certain.

Try it in a class. A typical school class of 30 or more has a good chance of containing two people with the same birthday.

On 18 August 1913, at the casino in Monte Carlo, the roulette ball landed on black again and again. As the streak grew, people rushed to bet huge sums on red, sure that it must be due. Black came up 26 times in a row.

A roulette wheel, like a coin, has no memory. Each spin is a fresh start. The mistake of thinking otherwise is now called the gambler's fallacy, or sometimes the Monte Carlo fallacy.

When a forecaster says there is a 70% chance of rain, it means that on days like this one, it rains about 7 times out of 10. [[@chance-weather|Weather chances]] come from computer models run many times with slightly different starting conditions.

Probability also explains why rare things still happen. A one-in-a-million event is unlikely for you today. But in a country of 140 crore people, it may happen to over a thousand of them.

text: Srinivasa Ramanujan was an [[@indian-mathematicians-modern|Indian mathematician]] who lived from 1887 to 1920. With little formal training, he discovered thousands of results about numbers, [[@fractions|fractions]] and [[@infinity|infinite]] sums. Some of his formulas were so unusual that experts at first could not tell how he found them.

In 1913 he wrote to the English mathematician G. H. Hardy at Cambridge University. Hardy invited him to England, and together they did important work. Ramanujan became one of the youngest Fellows of the Royal Society, Britain's top scientific academy. He died at just 32, but mathematicians are still exploring his notebooks today.

sec.t:
Ramanujan was born in Erode in 1887 and grew up in Kumbakonam, a temple town in Tamil Nadu. His family was poor. His father worked as a clerk in a cloth shop.

At about 15 he got hold of a book called A Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure and Applied Mathematics by G. S. Carr. It listed thousands of results with almost no explanations. Ramanujan worked through them all, then went far beyond. He filled notebooks with his own discoveries.

He won a scholarship to college but cared only about maths. He failed his other subjects, lost the scholarship and later failed again at another college. For years he had no degree and no job, and he kept working on slate and paper.

Ramanujan sailed for England in March 1914. A few months later the [[@world-war-one|First World War]] began. Food was rationed and Cambridge was cold and grey. Ramanujan was a strict [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]] and cooked for himself, often struggling to get the foods he was used to.

Still, the next few years were his most productive. With Hardy he found a way to count [[partition|partitions]], the number of ways a number can be written as a sum. For example, 4 can be made five ways: 4, 3+1, 2+2, 2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1. The numbers grow astonishingly fast, and their formula is one of the great results of the 20th century. In 1918 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College.

sec.h: The taxi and the lost notebook
sec.t:
Ramanujan fell seriously ill in England. Doctors at the time suspected [[@tb-india|tuberculosis]]. Some modern experts think it may have been a [[@liver|liver]] [[infection|infection]] caught in India. Hardy once visited him in hospital in a taxi numbered 1729 and said it seemed a dull number. Ramanujan replied that it was very interesting: the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two different ways.

He returned to India in 1919 and died in Kumbakonam in April 1920. In his last year he wrote about new functions that are still being studied. In 1976 an American mathematician, George Andrews, found a bundle of his last pages in a library at Trinity College, now called the "lost notebook". Ramanujan's formulas for [[@pi|pi]] are used in some of the fastest computer calculations of its digits. Ramanujan said his ideas came to him as gifts from Namagiri, his family goddess. Since 2012, India celebrates his birthday as National Mathematics Day.

text: In everyday life, people use "weight" and "mass" to mean the same thing. Scientists keep them apart.
**Mass** is how much matter, or stuff, something contains. It is measured in kilograms. Your mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon or floating in space.

**Weight** is how hard [[gravity|gravity]] pulls on that mass. It depends on where you are. On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth as strong as on Earth, so you'd [[@gravity-planets|weigh about one-sixth as much]]. On [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] you'd weigh more than twice as much. Scientists measure weight as a force, in units called newtons.
So when you step on a scale and it says 35 kg, it is really measuring how hard you press down, then turning that into kilograms using Earth's gravity.

st.prompt: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What is their mass on the Moon?

st.reveal: Mass is the amount of stuff in you, and that doesn't change when you travel. The astronaut still has a mass of 60 kg on the Moon. What changes is weight, because the Moon's gravity pulls only about one-sixth as hard.

sec.t:
Gravity depends on how much mass a planet has and how far you are from its centre. The Moon is much smaller than the Earth, so its pull is weaker.

When the Apollo astronauts walked on the [[@apollo-moon|Moon]] between 1969 and 1972, their [[@spacesuits|spacesuits]] and backpacks had a mass of around 80 kg. On Earth that would have been a crushing load. On the Moon it felt like carrying about 13 kg. The astronauts bounced and hopped across the surface, and sometimes fell over because they misjudged how their bodies would move.

Their mass hadn't changed. A heavy suit was still hard to start moving and hard to stop, even if it felt light to hold up.

Doctors on the space station still need to know if astronauts are losing or gaining mass. Ordinary scales don't work when everything is floating.

So NASA uses a device that measures mass instead. An astronaut holds on to a frame attached to [[@springs|a spring]]. The spring pushes them back and forth, and a computer measures how quickly they move. A bigger mass is harder to shake, so it moves more slowly. From that, the device works out the astronaut's mass in kilograms.

For 130 years, the kilogram was defined by a single metal cylinder about the size of a golf ball. It was made of platinum and [[iridium|iridium]] and kept under glass in a vault near [[@paris|Paris]]. People called it "Le Grand K". Countries kept official copies. India's is kept at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi.

The problem was that the cylinder could change. Comparisons over the years showed tiny differences between it and its copies, too small to see but enough to worry scientists.

On 20 May 2019, the kilogram was redefined using a fixed number from nature called the Planck constant. Now any well-equipped laboratory in the world can make a perfect kilogram without comparing it to a lump of metal. The kilogram became the last of the main [[@metric-system|metric units]] to be based on nature instead of an object.

When a shopkeeper weighs out a kilo of rice, the scale really measures how hard the rice pulls down. Since everyone in a market is on the same planet, it doesn't matter. Weight and mass go up and down together.

If you took that bag of rice to the Moon, a spring scale would show only about 170 grams. A balance scale, which compares the rice with standard weights, would still show 1 kg, because gravity pulls on both sides equally.

text: Archery is the sport of shooting arrows with a bow at a target. A bow is a spring. When the archer pulls back the string, the bent limbs of the bow store energy. When the string is released, that energy flings the arrow forwards at around 200 km/h.

In Olympic archery, archers shoot at a round target 70 metres away. The target has ten rings. The tiny gold centre is worth 10 points and is about 12 centimetres across, roughly the size of a CD. Hitting it again and again takes strength, perfect form and a very calm mind.

st.reveal: Arrows flex as they leave the bow, snaking around it before settling down. This is called the archer's paradox. Arrows are made with just the right stiffness, called spine, so the bend works out and they fly straight to the target.

sec.t:
People have used bows for tens of thousands of years. Stone points found in Sibudu Cave in South Africa, about 64,000 years old, may be the oldest arrowheads known. Bows let [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] hunters catch animals from a safe distance.

Later, bows were used in war. English longbowmen were famous at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Mongol riders shot arrows from galloping horses. In Japan, a style called kyudo turned archery into a calm, almost spiritual practice.

Olympic archers use the recurve bow, whose tips curve away from the archer. This shape stores more energy. The bow has a sight to help aim and stabiliser rods to keep it steady.

The compound bow, invented in the USA in the 1960s, uses wheels called cams and cables. It makes the bow easier to hold at full draw. Compound archery is not yet in the Olympics, but has its own world championships, and Indian compound archers such as Jyothi Surekha Vennam and Aditi Swami have won world titles.

sec.h: The science of a good shot
sec.t:
Every shot follows the same steps: stance, nock the arrow, draw, anchor the string at the chin, aim, release and follow through. Tiny differences matter. Over 70 metres, a wobble of a fraction of a millimetre at the bow can mean missing the gold.

Arrows begin to fall as soon as they leave the bow, so [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] must be allowed for. Wind pushes arrows sideways too. Archers train their breathing and try to keep their heart rate calm.

India has many fine archers. Deepika Kumari, the daughter of an autorickshaw driver in Jharkhand, became world number one in 2012. But India has not yet won an Olympic archery medal. In Paris in 2024, Dhiraj Bommadevara and Ankita Bhakat came fourth in the mixed team event.

In archery, the Paralympics brought a breakthrough. In 2024 [[@sport-paralympians-india|Harvinder Singh]] won India's first Paralympic archery gold. Sheetal Devi, born without arms, holds the bow with her foot and pulls the string back using her shoulder and a tab gripped in her mouth. She won bronze with Rakesh Kumar in the mixed team event, and photos of her shooting were shared around the world. In [[@bhutan|Bhutan]], archery is the national sport, and village contests come with songs, dances and cheerful teasing.

text: Major Dhyan Chand was an Indian field hockey player, and many people think he was the greatest ever. He won Olympic gold medals with India in 1928, 1932 and 1936, at a time when India was still under British rule. He was famous for his close control of the ball, his clever passes and the number of goals he scored.
He served in the Indian Army for most of his life and retired as a major. Today India's highest sports award is named after him, and his birthday, 29 August, is celebrated as National Sports Day.

sec.h: A soldier who played by moonlight
sec.t:
Dhyan Singh was born in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, in 1905. His father was in the army, and the family moved often. Dhyan joined the army himself at 16 and started playing hockey in regimental matches.

Soldiers worked during the day, so he often practised after duty. Stories say he trained under the [[@moon-phases|moon]], and friends nicknamed him "Chand", the Hindi word for moon. Whether or not that is exactly how it happened, the name became famous.

In 1936 Dhyan Chand was captain. The Berlin Olympics were run by Adolf Hitler's Nazi government, which used the Games to show off its power. India lost a warm-up match to Germany, but in the final they beat the hosts 8–1.

Dhyan Chand is said to have taken off his heavy boots and played barefoot or in rubber shoes in the second half, because the ground was wet. He was among India's scorers in the final. Three years later, [[@world-war-two|World War Two]] began and the Olympics stopped until 1948.

Many stories are told about Dhyan Chand. One says officials in the Netherlands broke his stick to check for a magnet. Another says Hitler offered him German citizenship. These are retold everywhere, but historians have not found reliable evidence for them.

His goal total is also uncertain. Numbers like 400 or even 1,000 goals are quoted, but many matches had no proper records. What the Olympic results show clearly is that he scored a lot, in the biggest games, and that his teammates and opponents spoke of him with awe.

Dhyan Chand died in Delhi in 1979. The National Stadium in Delhi was renamed after him in 2002. In 2021 India's top sports award, the Khel Ratna, was renamed the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna.

Some fans have campaigned for years for him to receive the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award. He received the Padma Bhushan in 1956. His son Ashok Kumar also played hockey for India and scored the winning goal in the 1975 World Cup final, so the family's story continued on the field. Hockey then was played on grass, and the game has since moved to artificial turf, which is faster and flatter.

text: [[@oddity-ancient-olympics-weird|The ancient Olympic Games]] began in Olympia, Greece, traditionally in 776 BCE. They were held every four years for over 1,000 years. Athletes ran races, wrestled, threw the discus and raced [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]]. Winners got a crown of olive leaves.

The modern Olympics started in Athens in 1896, led by a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin. Today the Summer Games bring together over 10,000 athletes from more than 200 teams, and the Winter Games, first held in 1924, add skiing, skating and ice hockey.

sec.t:
The Games were held at Olympia in honour of Zeus, king of the [[@greek-myths|Greek gods]]. For the first few Games, there may have been only one event: a sprint of one length of the stadium, about 192 metres, called the stadion. Over time, events were added: longer races, boxing, wrestling, a race in armour and chariot racing.

Only free Greek men and boys could compete, and most athletes competed naked. Married women were not allowed to watch. Yet a Spartan princess named Kyniska became an Olympic champion, because in chariot races the prize went to the owner of the horses, not the driver. Her team won in 396 BCE and again four years later.

The ancient Games faded away in the late 300s CE, when the Roman Empire turned Christian and pagan festivals were ended. For about 1,500 years, there were none.

The five rings were designed in 1913. Coubertin said every country's flag of the time had at least one of the six colours: blue, yellow, black, green, red and the white background. The rings first flew at the 1920 Games in Antwerp, Belgium.

sec.h: India and the USA at the Olympics
sec.t:
India first sent a proper team in 1920. Its [[@hockey-rules|hockey teams]] won eight Olympic gold medals, starting in 1928, led by players such as [[@dhyan-chand|Dhyan Chand]]. Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual gold in shooting in 2008, and [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] won gold in javelin at the Tokyo Games, then silver in Paris in 2024. At Paris, shooter Manu Bhaker won two bronze medals, the first Indian since independence to win two medals at one Games.

The USA has won more Olympic medals than any other country, and [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]] hosts the Summer Games in 2028. Those Games will include [[@cricket-history|cricket]], for the first time since 1900, when Britain beat France in Paris in the only Olympic cricket match ever played.

The fastest humans reach about 44 km/h. Some [[@fastest-animal|animals]] are far, far faster. A cheetah can sprint at up to about 100 km/h for a short burst, more than twice [[@usain-bolt|Usain Bolt]]'s top speed. During a sprint, a trained athlete's [[@heart-beat|heart]] can beat close to 200 times a minute, pumping blood to [[@muscles|muscles]] that burn energy fast.

text: A TV station sends its programmes up to a satellite in space using a big dish on the ground. The satellite catches the signal, boosts it and beams it back down over a huge area, sometimes a whole country or more. The dish on a roof or balcony catches that faint signal and passes it to a box that turns it into pictures and sound.

The clever part is where the satellite sits. TV satellites [[orbit|orbit]] about 35,786 km above the [[equator|equator]], where one trip round the Earth takes almost exactly a day. So from the ground, the satellite never seems to move, and the dish can stay fixed.

st.reveal: TV satellites orbit at just the right height to go round once every 24 hours, matching the Earth's spin. From the ground they seem to hang still, so the dish can stay pointed at one place.

sec.h: The parking spot in the sky
sec.t:
Most satellites go round the Earth much faster than once a day. The International Space Station, for example, circles every 90 minutes or so. The higher a satellite goes, the slower it moves, because [[@gravity-planets|gravity]] is weaker further away.

At about 35,786 km, one orbit lasts 24 hours. This is called a geostationary orbit, meaning "staying still over the Earth". The writer Arthur C. Clarke described it in a magazine article in 1945. He suggested that three satellites spaced around the equator could send radio and TV to almost the whole planet. Because of him, this orbit is sometimes called the Clarke orbit.

The first satellite to relay live TV across the Atlantic was Telstar, in July 1962. It wasn't geostationary, so each broadcast lasted only as long as Telstar was passing overhead, about 20 minutes at a time. In 1964, a geostationary satellite called Syncom 3 carried pictures of the Tokyo Olympics to the United States.

India's own story began with the SITE experiment of 1975, which beamed [[@doordarshan-tech|lessons to villages]] using a borrowed NASA satellite. Today, India's GSAT and INSAT satellites, built by ISRO, carry many of the country's TV channels.

In India, private direct-to-home, or DTH, services started in 2003. Before that, most homes got satellite channels through a local cable operator. The operator had a large dish and ran wires along lanes and up the walls of buildings. DTH gave each home its own small dish, usually about 60 centimetres across.

Doordarshan launched its free DTH service, now called DD Free Dish, in 2004. Families buy the dish and box once and then watch dozens of channels without a monthly bill. It is popular in villages and hill areas that are hard to reach by cable.

Satellite TV has one weakness. Heavy rain can freeze or blank the picture for a few minutes. Raindrops absorb and scatter the high-frequency [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] that carry the signal, an effect engineers call rain fade. During a strong [[@monsoon|monsoon]] downpour, many Indian families know to wait it out.

There is a stranger glitch too. Twice a year, around the [[equinox|equinoxes]], the Sun passes directly behind the satellite as seen from a dish. For a few minutes each day, the Sun's radio noise drowns out the signal.

text: A self-driving car "sees" with several kinds of [[sensor|sensors]] at once. [[@cameras-how|Cameras]] read lane lines, signs and traffic lights. Radar bounces [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] off other cars to tell how fast they are moving, even in fog. Many cars also carry lidar, a spinning sensor that fires [[@lasers|laser]] pulses and times their [[@echoes|echoes]] to build a 3D picture of everything nearby.

A powerful computer in the car combines all this into one picture. It labels each object (car, cyclist, kerb), guesses what each will do next, and then plans how to steer, speed up or brake. It repeats this many times every second.

st.prompt: A self-driving car has cameras. Why do many also carry lidar, which fires laser pulses?

options.t: Lidar measures exactly how far away things are, even in the dark
Lidar lets the car see through walls and buildings
Lidar is used to warn other drivers, like a flashing light

st.reveal: A camera sees colours and shapes but can be fooled about distance, and it struggles at night. Lidar times how long each laser pulse takes to bounce back, so the car knows how far away every object is, light or dark.

n.certNote: The technology is real and already in use in some cities. Experts disagree about how quickly it will spread, how safe it is compared with human drivers, and whether it can cope with very crowded, unpredictable roads.

sec.h: A desert race that went wrong
sec.t:
In 2004, the US military research agency DARPA set a challenge. It offered a million dollars to any robot car that could cross about 240 km (150 miles) of the Mojave Desert. Not one finished. The best car got only about 12 km before it got stuck on a rock.

A year later, in a second race, five cars made it to the end. The winner, a modified car from Stanford University called Stanley, crossed the line in under seven hours. Many of the engineers from those races went on to build today's self-driving cars.

Those early cars were covered in sensors and packed with computers that filled the boot. Today the computers are much smaller, but the basic recipe is the same: see, place yourself, predict, then plan.

The hardest part is not spotting a pedestrian. It is predicting what that person will do. Will the child on the pavement chase the ball? Will the cyclist swerve around a pothole?

To learn this, companies use [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] trained on millions of kilometres of real driving. The computer studies how people, cars and bikes usually behave, and it plans for the most likely moves and the dangerous ones too.

Driverless taxis already run in some US cities, including Phoenix and San Francisco, where wide roads, clear markings and steady weather help. Riders call one with an app, and no one sits behind the wheel.

Indian roads are a much harder test. A single street in Bengaluru might hold autorickshaws, scooters [[weaving|weaving]] between buses, a cow resting in the middle and a wedding procession. Lane markings may be faded, and drivers talk with their horns. Engineers say a car that can drive well there will be able to drive almost anywhere. Nobody yet knows when that will be.

Engineers sort driving help into levels from 0 to 5. Level 5 means a car that needs no human anywhere, in any weather. No such car exists yet. Most cars with driver-assist features today sit at level 2, where the car can steer and brake on a highway but a person must keep watching. The driverless taxis are level 4: no driver, but only inside areas their companies have mapped and tested carefully.

text: Space is a harsh place. [[@rockets-how|Rockets]] shake violently, temperatures swing wildly and every gram costs money to launch. Solving those problems forces engineers to invent new materials, [[sensor|sensors]] and machines. Many of those inventions later find jobs on Earth.

The best known examples are memory foam, the tiny camera sensor in your phone, better ways to [[@water-purify|clean water]] and lighter, tougher materials. Just as important are the satellites themselves. They help forecast storms, guide ships, plan crops and tell your phone where you are.

st.reveal: Memory foam was made for NASA aircraft seats in 1966. Velcro was invented by a Swiss engineer after a walk with his dog, and Teflon was discovered by accident at a chemical company in 1938. NASA used both, which is how the mix-up started.

sec.t:
In 1966, an engineer named Charles Yost, working with NASA's Ames Research Center, made a foam that slowly moulds to a body and then springs back. It was meant to make aircraft seats safer in a crash. It is now found in mattresses, pillows, shoes and [[@helmets|sports helmets]].

For the Apollo [[@moon-landing-sites|Moon landings]], the tool company Black & Decker designed a battery-powered drill that astronauts could use to pull up samples of Moon rock. What the company learned helped shape cordless tools and small [[@vacuum-cleaners|handheld vacuum cleaners]]. NASA research also helped create scratch-resistant coatings now used on [[@lenses-glasses|glasses]].

Some of the biggest benefits came from what satellites can see. Weather satellites watch clouds and storms grow over the oceans, so [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] can warn coastal towns days before [[@cyclones-india|a cyclone arrives]]. The [[@gps-how|GPS]] system, built by the United States, now guides everything from delivery riders to farm tractors.

India's space agency, ISRO, built its programme around this idea from the start. Satellites help map groundwater, track crops and monitor forests. Indian ocean scientists use satellite readings of sea temperature and colour to send fishermen daily advice on where fish are likely to gather, which can save fuel and time at sea.

The same satellites watch for disasters. When Cyclone Phailin approached the coast of Odisha in 2013, satellite images and forecasts helped officials move close to a million people to shelters before it struck. Far fewer lives were lost than in a similar [[cyclone|cyclone]] in 1999. Tools built for space ended up guarding fishing villages.

Space programmes get credit for some things they never made. Velcro came from a Swiss engineer who noticed burrs sticking to his dog's fur, and it was patented in the 1950s. [[@velcro|Velcro]] became famous partly because astronauts used it to stop things floating away. [[@accident-teflon|Non-stick Teflon]] and the orange drink powder Tang have the same story.

NASA publishes a yearly report called Spinoff that lists technologies traced back to its work. It has been printed every year since 1976 and now includes more than 2,000 examples. Many are humble: better insulation, cleaner water filters, safer [[@jobs-firefighter|firefighters]]' masks.

text: Ancient China gave the world many inventions, but four are so famous that they are called the Four Great Inventions: paper, the magnetic compass, gunpowder and printing. Each spread slowly westward along trade routes and changed how people wrote, travelled, fought and shared ideas.

China also gave the world [[@silk|silk]], porcelain, tea drinking, kites, the wheelbarrow, cast iron and an early earthquake detector. Many of these came from more than 2,000 years of record-keeping, careful craftsmanship and government support for scholars and engineers.

st.prompt: The oldest dated printed book in the world was made in China in 868 CE. What was it?

options.t: A Buddhist holy text first written in India
A cookbook for the emperor
A map of the Great Wall

st.reveal: It is a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist teaching that began in India and was translated into Chinese. It was printed from carved wooden blocks onto a scroll about 5 metres long. It was found in a sealed cave near Dunhuang and is now in the British Library.

sec.t:
Before paper, Chinese scribes wrote on strips of [[@bamboo|bamboo]] tied together, or on silk, which was costly. Bamboo books were heavy. One story says an official needed two men to carry the reports he wrote to the emperor.

Early forms of paper existed by the 100s BCE. In 105 CE, an official named Cai Lun presented the emperor with an improved way of making it. Tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets were soaked, pounded and spread thin to dry. [[@paper-invention|Paper]] was cheap and light, and its use spread across China, then to [[@ancient-korea|Korea]], Japan, the Islamic world and, by about the 1100s, to Europe.

Chinese thinkers noticed that a lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, always turned to point north and south. More than 2,000 years ago, they made spoon-shaped lodestones that spun on a smooth plate. These were used at first for fortune-telling and for planning buildings.

By the 1000s CE, Chinese sailors were using magnetised needles to find their way at sea when clouds hid the stars. The scholar Shen Kuo described such a needle in 1088. It works because Earth itself acts like a giant [[@magnets-how|magnet]].

Alchemists in the 800s CE mixed saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal while searching for medicines and a potion for long life. Instead, the mixture flared and burned. A military book from 1044 CE gives the first known written recipe.

At first, gunpowder was used in fire arrows and simple bombs, and later in [[@rockets-how|rockets]] and guns. It also gave the world [[@fireworks|fireworks]], which are still lit to celebrate Chinese [[@new-year|New Year]], Diwali and the Fourth of July.

In 132 CE, the scholar Zhang Heng built a large bronze vessel with eight dragons around the top, each holding a ball in its mouth. Below sat eight bronze toads with open mouths. When the ground shook, even far away, a ball dropped from one dragon into a toad, showing the direction of the earthquake. Nobody knows exactly how the inside worked, and modern engineers have built several possible versions.

China and India swapped ideas for centuries. Buddhism travelled from India to China, and Chinese monks such as Xuanzang walked across mountains and deserts in the 600s CE to study at [[@nalanda|Nalanda]]. He carried hundreds of texts home. Paper and silk, in turn, made their way to India.

text: Gladiators were trained fighters who battled in Roman arenas to entertain huge crowds. Most were enslaved people, prisoners of war or criminals. Some were free men who signed up for money and fame. They lived in special training schools, ate a carefully planned diet and practised every day.

Life was hard and dangerous, but it wasn't always the bloodbath of films. Gladiators were costly to train, so many fights stopped before anyone died. A popular gladiator could become a celebrity, with fans scratching his name on walls. A few even won their freedom.

st.prompt: How often did a gladiator fight end with someone killed?

options.t: Less often than films suggest, perhaps one fight in five or ten
Every single fight, always to the death
Never, it was all pretend

st.reveal: Gladiators were expensive to train, so owners didn't want them killed. Historians estimate that in the 1st century CE, perhaps 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 fights ended in a death, though it varied over time.

myth: The crowd gave a thumbs down to call for a gladiator's death.

Romans did use thumb signals, but nobody knows exactly what they meant. Some historians think a turned thumb meant death and a hidden thumb meant mercy. The famous "thumbs down" comes mostly from a 19th-century painting.

sec.t:
Gladiators lived in barracks called *ludi*. Next to the Colosseum stood the biggest, the Ludus Magnus, with its own small practice arena. Trainers taught each fighter a style, with specific weapons and armour. They practised with wooden swords against posts and each other.

Doctors looked after them. The famous doctor Galen began his career treating gladiators in what is now Turkey. He wrote that good care meant fewer deaths, which pleased the owners.

In 1993, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found a gladiator graveyard at Ephesus, an ancient city in Turkey. Studies of the bones in 2014 showed that gladiators ate mostly barley and beans. Roman writers called them *hordearii*, or "barley men".

Their bones also had lots of strontium, which suggests they drank a tonic made of plant ash. Roman writers mention this drink. It may have helped strengthen [[@bones|bones]] that took a beating. A diet rich in grains might also have added a layer of fat, which could have protected them from cuts.

A big show began in the morning with animal hunts. Lions, bears and even elephants were brought from across the [[empire|empire]]. At midday, criminals were executed. The main gladiator fights came in the afternoon.

The [[@colosseum|Colosseum]] opened in 80 CE and could hold about 50,000 people, more than many cricket grounds in India today. A huge awning shaded the crowd. Free food and prizes were sometimes thrown into the stands.

A gladiator who survived years of fights might be given a wooden sword called a *rudis*, a sign of freedom. Some stayed on as trainers. Fans wrote graffiti about their favourites on the walls of Pompeii, praising their skill and good looks.

Not every gladiator accepted his fate. In 73 BCE, a Thracian gladiator named Spartacus broke out of a school in Capua with about 70 others. Their revolt grew into an army of tens of thousands before Rome crushed it in 71 BCE.

There were a few women gladiators. A carving from Halicarnassus, now in the British Museum, shows two women fighters named Amazon and Achillia. Emperor Septimius Severus banned female gladiators around 200 CE.

The games faded as the empire became Christian and grew poorer, and they ended in the early 400s. Fighting for crowds didn't disappear, though. In India, traditional [[@wrestling-india|wrestling]] in mud pits, called kushti, has drawn cheering crowds for centuries.

text: Lal Bahadur Shastri was India's second full-time prime minister, after Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]]. He led the country from June 1964 until his sudden death in January 1966. In that short time, India fought a war with Pakistan and faced a serious shortage of food.

Shastri was small, quiet and famously honest. He came from a poor family and lived simply even in high office. His slogan "Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan", meaning "Hail the soldier, hail the farmer", honoured the two groups he believed India depended on most. He also backed changes in farming and dairy that helped India grow far more food in the years after his death.

sec.t:
Shastri was born on 2 October 1904, sharing a birthday with Gandhi, in Mughalsarai, near [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]. His father died when he was a baby, and his mother raised him with help from relatives. Money was tight.

An often-told story says he sometimes swam across the Ganga to get to school, because he couldn't spare the money for the boat. Whether or not every detail is true, it fits what people knew of him: stubborn, hard-working and not one to complain.

His family name was Srivastava, but he dropped it as a young man because he disliked the caste system. "Shastri" was a title he earned in 1925 after graduating from Kashi Vidyapith, a college set up by nationalists in Varanasi.

At 16, Shastri left his studies to join Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement. Over the next 25 years he was jailed several times by the British, spending years of his life in prison.

After independence, he became a minister in Uttar Pradesh and then in Nehru's government in Delhi. As railway minister, he made a decision people still talk about. In 1956, after a deadly train accident at Ariyalur in Tamil Nadu, he resigned, saying he took moral responsibility. The [[@indian-railways|railways]] were vast and he hadn't caused the crash, but he felt the minister should answer for it.

When Nehru died in 1964, Shastri became prime minister. A year later, war broke out with Pakistan. Shastri's calm leadership during the fighting earned him great respect across India.

At the same time, [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains failed and food ran short. India was relying on wheat shipped from the USA. Shastri asked Indians to skip one meal a week to save grain, and he had his own family do it first. In 1965 he gave the slogan "Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan", linking the soldiers at the border with the farmers in the fields.

He supported new seeds and farming methods that later grew into the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]], which made India far better at feeding itself.

In January 1966, Shastri travelled to Tashkent, then part of the Soviet Union, for peace talks with Pakistan's president, Ayub Khan. On 10 January they signed the Tashkent Declaration, agreeing to pull back their armies. In the early hours of the next morning, Shastri died. The official cause was a heart attack, though some people, including members of his family, have long raised questions.

His body was flown home, and huge crowds lined the streets of Delhi. He was given the Bharat Ratna that year, the first person to receive it after death. His memorial in Delhi is called Vijay Ghat, meaning "place of victory".

text: Seattle is a city in Washington state, in the far north-west of the US, built on hills between a long inlet of the Pacific called Puget Sound and a large freshwater lake. On clear days, snowy volcanoes and mountains appear on the horizon. It's famous for its Space Needle tower, its coffee shops, its seafood market, its music and its technology companies.

Seattle is also known for its grey, drizzly weather. In fact, it gets less rain than many US cities, about 950 mm a year, but the rain falls gently, on many days, mostly from autumn to spring. The damp, mild [[climate|climate]] keeps everything green, which is why Washington's nickname is the Evergreen State.

st.reveal: Miami gets about 1,500 mm a year, much of it in short, heavy storms. Seattle gets about 950 mm, but spread over many grey, drizzly days, especially from October to April. That's why it feels so rainy.
