myth: Seattle is the rainiest city in the United States.

Many US cities, including New York, Miami, Houston and New Orleans, get more rain in a year. Seattle has many cloudy, drizzly days, which gives it its reputation, but its summers are usually dry and sunny.

sec.t:
Long before settlers arrived, the land around Seattle was home to Coast Salish peoples, including the Duwamish and Suquamish. They fished for salmon and built cedar longhouses. In the 1850s, American settlers founded a town and named it after a local leader, Si'ahl, whose name became "Seattle" in English.

The Duwamish and other [[@native-nations|native nations]] lost most of their land as the city grew. Today, their [[descendant|descendants]] still live in the area, and Coast Salish art and canoe journeys are an important part of the region's life.

The Space Needle was built for the 1962 World's Fair, when the city wanted to show off a futuristic image. It is about 184 m tall, roughly the height of a 50-storey building, with a viewing deck near the top.

At Pike Place Market, open since 1907, fishmongers famously throw whole salmon to each other across the counter when customers buy them. Seattle also has some of the longest floating bridges in the world. Because Lake Washington is too deep and its bed too soft for normal bridge supports, the road rests on huge hollow concrete pontoons that [[@floating-ships|float]] on the water.

On a clear day, Mount Rainier rises about 4,392 m to the south-east, covered in [[glacier|glaciers]]. It's an active [[@volcano|volcano]] and is watched closely by scientists, because mudflows from an eruption could reach towns in the valleys. Orcas swim in Puget Sound, and visitors take boat trips to see them. Scientists have studied the sound "[[dialect|dialects]]" of these orca families, which differ from pod to pod.

Seattle also has a big place in music history. Jimi Hendrix, one of the most famous guitarists ever, grew up in Seattle. In the early 1990s, local bands such as Nirvana and Pearl Jam made a raw, loud style of [[@rock-music|rock]] called grunge, and the city's name became known to teenagers around the world.

text: Times Square is a busy junction in the middle of Manhattan, in [[@new-york|New York]] City, where two big streets, Broadway and Seventh Avenue, cross. It's famous for giant glowing screens that cover the buildings from street to rooftop, for its theatres and for the ball that drops on New Year's Eve.

About 220,000 people walked into Times Square on an average day in 2024, and on the busiest days far more. Many are tourists, some are office workers rushing to the subway, and some are theatre fans heading to a show. It's often called the Crossroads of the World.

myth: The Times Square ball has dropped every New Year's Eve since 1907.
It didn't drop in 1942 or 1943. During the Second World War, the city's lights were dimmed, and crowds marked midnight with a minute of silence instead.

sec.t:
The area used to be called Longacre Square, and it was known for horse stables and carriage makers. In 1904 *The New York Times* moved into a tall new tower at the south end of the square. The city renamed the square after the [[@newspapers|newspaper]], and a new subway station opened beneath it that same year.

To celebrate its new home, the *Times* held a New Year's Eve party with fireworks at the end of 1904. When fireworks were banned, it came up with a different idea.

On the last night of 1907, a ball made of iron and wood, covered in 100 [[@light-bulb|light bulbs]], was lowered down a pole on the tower. It reached the bottom exactly at midnight. The tradition has continued almost every year since.

The exceptions were 1942 and 1943. During the Second World War, New York dimmed its lights at night in case of enemy attack, so the ball stayed dark. Crowds still gathered at midnight. They stood for a minute of silence, and chimes rang out from a sound truck parked below the tower. The ball returned, glowing, at the end of 1944.

Today's ball is far bigger and covered in thousands of crystal triangles and LED lights. Around a million people often pack the streets to watch, and many more see it on television. It's one of the most famous ways to see in the [[@new-year|New Year]] anywhere.

{{story:broadway}}

Times Square glows all night. That's partly because New York's planning rules require buildings in the area to carry large, lit-up signs. Companies pay huge sums to put their [[@advertising|adverts]] on these screens, because so many people look up at them.

Some screens wrap around corners or stretch many storeys high. A few are among the largest in the world. On a cloudy night, the glow can light up the clouds above. Each screen is carefully timed, and adverts change every few seconds so the whole square seems to flicker and move.

Times Square sits at the heart of New York's Theatre District. Dozens of theatres nearby put on [[@broadway|Broadway]] shows, the long-running musicals and plays that draw audiences from around the world. Some shows have run for decades.

The neighbourhood hasn't always been glamorous. By the 1970s parts of it were run-down and many people felt unsafe there. In the 1990s the city and businesses cleaned it up, and big shops, restaurants and hotels moved in.

For decades Times Square was jammed with cars, and people squeezed along crowded pavements. In 2009 the city closed parts of Broadway to traffic and turned them into pedestrian plazas with chairs and benches. Some people predicted traffic chaos, but road injuries fell and the plazas filled up.

Times Square is still noisy and packed, with street performers, people dressed as cartoon characters and crowds taking photos. Some New Yorkers try to avoid it, while visitors from Mumbai to Melbourne put it at the top of their list.

text: Washington, D.C. became the capital because of a deal. After the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]], the new government owed huge war debts. Alexander Hamilton, from the North, wanted the national government to take over states' debts. Southern leaders such as [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] and James Madison didn't like the plan. In 1790, at a dinner arranged by Jefferson, they reached a compromise: the South would support Hamilton's debt plan, and the capital would be built in the South, on the Potomac River.
Congress passed the Residence Act in 1790. President [[@george-washington|George Washington]] chose the exact site, and the city was named after him. The government moved in in 1800.

myth: A law says no building in Washington may be taller than the Capitol.
The Height of Buildings Act of 1910 limits buildings mostly by the width of the street they stand on. The result is a low skyline, but the rule is about street width, not the Capitol dome.

sec.t:
The [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]] called for a special [[federal|federal]] district that belonged to no state, so no single state could control the national government. Maryland and Virginia gave land for a square of about 260 km², tilted like a diamond. In 1846 the Virginia part was given back.

D.C. stands for District of Columbia. Its residents can vote for president, but they have no voting member in [[@congress-usa|Congress]]. Some people want D.C. to become a state, while others argue it should stay a federal district. Its car number plates carry the words "End Taxation Without Representation". That echoes a slogan from the American Revolution, when colonists complained about paying taxes to a British [[parliament|parliament]] they had no vote in.

At the heart of the city is the National Mall, a long lawn running about 3 km from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial. The Washington Monument stands in the middle. When it was finished in 1884, it was the tallest structure in the world, until the [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] passed it in 1889.

On 28 August 1963, about 250,000 people gathered on the Mall for the March on Washington. From the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, [[@martin-luther-king|Martin Luther King Jr]] gave his [[@speeches-famous|"I Have a Dream" speech]].

Along the Mall stand the museums of the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]] Institution, most of them free. It began with money left by James Smithson, a British scientist who had never visited America. The National Air and Space Museum holds the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]]' first plane and an Apollo spacecraft. The National Museum of Natural History holds the Hope Diamond. These [[@museums|museums]] welcome millions of visitors a year.

sec.h: Cherry blossoms and a low skyline
sec.t: In 1912, the city of Tokyo gave Washington about 3,000 cherry trees. Every spring they bloom around a lake called the Tidal Basin, and a festival celebrates them. Because of a 1910 law limiting building heights, the city has no skyscrapers. The Washington Monument still rises above almost everything.

text: Chinese legends are stories told for thousands of years about how the world began, why the Moon glows and how heroes outwitted gods. They include the giant Pangu, whose body became mountains and rivers, and Nüwa, a goddess who shaped the first people from yellow clay.

The best-loved tales star an archer who saved Earth from scorching heat, a goddess who lives on the Moon, and a cheeky Monkey King. These stories are still told at festivals, in films, comics and cartoons, from Beijing to Singapore.

myth: Chinese dragons are fierce fire-breathing monsters, like the ones in European stories.
In Chinese legends, dragons are usually wise and kind. They live in rivers, seas and clouds, and control rain. Emperors used the dragon as their symbol of power and good fortune.

sec.t:
One story says that in the beginning, everything was mixed up inside a giant cosmic egg. Inside slept a giant called Pangu. When he woke, he cracked the egg. The light, clear part rose to become the sky, and the heavy, dark part sank to become the Earth.

Pangu stood between them, pushing them apart, growing taller each day for 18,000 years. When he finally died, his breath became the wind, his voice thunder, his eyes the Sun and Moon, and his blood the rivers.

sec.h: Ten suns and a lonely goddess
sec.t:
Long ago, the story goes, there were ten suns, the sons of a god. They took turns crossing the sky, one each day. But one day, all ten rose at once. Crops burned and rivers dried up.

A great archer, Hou Yi, shot down nine of them with his arrows, leaving one sun to light the world. As a reward, he received a potion of everlasting life. His wife, Chang'e, drank it, and floated up to the Moon, where she lives with a white Jade Rabbit.

At the Mid-Autumn Festival, families eat mooncakes and gaze at the full moon, looking for Chang'e and her rabbit. China has named its Moon missions after her. In 2019, *Chang'e 4* became the first spacecraft to land on the [[@moon-far-side|Moon's far side]].

{{story:moon-far-side}}

The most famous hero of all is Sun Wukong, the Monkey King. Born from a stone, he learns magic, can leap thousands of kilometres in one somersault and has a staff that shrinks to the size of a needle.

He causes chaos in heaven, defeats armies of celestial soldiers and is finally trapped under a mountain for 500 years. To make up for it, he must guard a monk on a dangerous journey to the west.

His adventures fill *Journey to the West*, a long novel from the 1500s and one of China's great classic books. Some scholars think the Monkey King may have been partly inspired by stories of [[@myths-hanuman|Hanuman]] that reached China through trade and Buddhism. Others think he grew from Chinese folk tales. The question is still open.

The novel's monk is based on a real man, Xuanzang. In about 629 CE, he left China and travelled over deserts and mountains to India, hunting for Buddhist books.

He studied for years at [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], the great university in what is now Bihar. When he returned to China around 645, he carried hundreds of texts and spent the rest of his life translating them. His travel record is still one of our best descriptions of 7th-century India.

sec.h: Dragons and a monster called Nian
sec.t:
Chinese dragons are long, snake-like and usually kind. They live in seas, rivers and clouds, and bring rain to farms. Emperors used the dragon as their symbol.

Another tale explains Chinese New Year. A beast called Nian came each year to eat crops and frighten villagers. But it was scared of loud noises and the colour red. So people hung red papers and lit firecrackers, and the festival's noisy, red celebrations began.

One of the gentlest legends tells of a cowherd and a weaver girl who fell in love but were separated by the Milky Way, a river in the sky. Once a year, magpies form a bridge so they can meet. The pair are the stars Altair and Vega.

That night is celebrated as Qixi, sometimes called Chinese Valentine's Day. Like many of the world's oldest stories, it looks up at the sky and finds a reason for what it sees, much as [[@myths-dragons|dragon legends]] found reasons for rain and storms.

text: The Thirukkural, often just called the Kural, is a book of 1,330 short poems written in Tamil by a poet called [[@thiruvalluvar|Thiruvalluvar]]. Each poem is a two-line [[couplet|couplet]] of only seven words. Together they give advice on how to live well: how to be good, how to run a home or a country, and how to love.
It is one of the most loved books in [[@tamil-ancient|Tamil]] and has been read for more than 1,500 years. Children in Tamil Nadu learn kurals by heart at school.

options.t: Love
Gods and heaven

st.reveal: The third part, Inbam, is about love between couples, in 250 couplets. Many people who know only the moral sayings are surprised to find it there.

myth: The Thirukkural is only a book of moral rules.
The first two parts give advice on right living, friendship, money and leadership. The whole third part is love poetry about two people falling in love and missing each other.

sec.t:
Every kural follows the same strict pattern, called a metre: four word-units in the first line and three in the second. That makes them easy to remember and hard to forget.

The book is split into 133 chapters, each with exactly ten kurals on one subject, such as patience, [[@gratitude|gratitude]], friendship, learning or not gossiping. The first and largest groups are about virtue (Aram) and wealth (Porul). The last, about love, is called Inbam.

The very first kural says that just as the letter A comes first among letters, God comes first in the world. Kural 391 gives advice students still quote: learn thoroughly what you should learn, then live by it. Another says that friendship is not for laughing together, but for stepping in to scold a friend who is going wrong. A whole chapter praises farmers, saying that wherever the world wanders, it follows the plough.

Nobody knows for sure. Stories say he was a weaver from Mylapore, now part of [[@chennai|Chennai]], and that his wife Vasuki was famous for her patience. These are traditions, not records.

Even his date is argued over. Some scholars place him around 300 BCE, while many put the Kural somewhere around the 5th century CE. The book itself names no king, no city and no particular religion. Because of this, people of many faiths, and none, have claimed it as their own.

Tamil Nadu celebrates Thiruvalluvar Day in January, during the Pongal holidays. The [[@governors-states|state government]] even uses a Thiruvalluvar calendar, which counts its years from a traditional date for his birth, 31 BCE.

{{story:onam-pongal}}

Christian missionaries translated parts of the Kural into Latin in the 1700s. G. U. Pope, a missionary who loved Tamil, published a full English version in 1886. Today there are [[@translation|translations]] in dozens of languages, from Hindi to French and Chinese.

The Russian writer Leo Tolstoy read the Kural in German. In 1908 he quoted it in a long letter to an Indian reader, arguing for answering violence with love. A lawyer working in [[@south-africa|South Africa]] read that letter and printed it. His name was Mohandas [[@gandhi|Gandhi]].

sec.h: The Kural all around Tamil Nadu
sec.t:
Look up inside a Tamil Nadu government bus and you may see a kural painted above the windows. They appear on walls, in court judgements and in speeches in [[@parliament-india|Parliament]].

On 1 January 2000, a stone statue of Thiruvalluvar was unveiled on a rock off [[@kanyakumari|Kanyakumari]], at India's southern tip. It is 133 feet (about 40 metres) tall, matching the 133 chapters. Its pedestal is 38 feet, the number of chapters on virtue. Few books have ever been measured in stone. The Kural is one of the oldest examples of [[@poetry|poetry]] as practical advice, and much of it still fits a modern school day.

text: चॉकलेट कोको के पेड़ के बीजों से बनती है। खेत पर इन बीजों को, जिन्हें बीन्स कहते हैं, सफ़ेद गूदे समेत फलियों से निकाला जाता है। फिर उन्हें लगभग एक हफ़्ते तक ढेर में रखकर [[fermentation|ख़मीर उठने]] दिया जाता है, और फिर धूप में सुखाया जाता है। इसके बाद ही उनमें चॉकलेट का स्वाद आना शुरू होता है।

फ़ैक्टरी में बीन्स को भूना जाता है, तोड़ा जाता है और उनके छिलके उतारे जाते हैं। बचे हुए टुकड़ों को निब्स कहते हैं। इन्हें पीसकर एक गाढ़ा लेप बनाया जाता है, जिसे कोको मास कहते हैं। इसमें चीनी, थोड़ा और [[@food-science-chocolate-melt|कोको बटर]] और कभी-कभी दूध का पाउडर मिलाया जाता है। मशीनें इस मिश्रण को घंटों पीसती और चलाती हैं, ताकि यह मुलायम हो जाए। आख़िर में इसकी टेम्परिंग होती है, इसे साँचों में डाला जाता है और ठंडा करके बार बना ली जाती है।

sec.t:
ताज़े कोको बीन्स कड़वे होते हैं और उनमें चॉकलेट का ज़रा भी स्वाद नहीं होता। खेत पर बीन्स और गूदे का ढेर केले के पत्तों से ढक दिया जाता है या लकड़ी के बक्सों में भर दिया जाता है। [[microbe|सूक्ष्मजीव]] मीठे गूदे को खाने लगते हैं, ढेर गर्म हो जाता है, और बीन्स के अंदर रासायनिक बदलाव शुरू हो जाते हैं।

लगभग पाँच से सात दिन बाद बीन्स को सूखने के लिए फैला दिया जाता है। फिर उन्हें बोरियों में भरकर फ़ैक्टरियों तक भेजा जाता है। दुनिया का ज़्यादातर कोको पश्चिमी अफ़्रीका के छोटे किसान उगाते हैं, ख़ासकर [[@chocolate-world|कोत दिव्वार और घाना]] में।

1828 में नीदरलैंड्स के रसायनशास्त्री कोनराड फ़ान हाउटेन ने एक ऐसी प्रेस बनाई जो कोको से उसकी हल्की पीली चिकनाई, यानी कोको बटर, निचोड़ लेती थी। पीछे कोको पाउडर बच जाता था। 1847 में इंग्लैंड की कंपनी जे.एस. फ़्राई एंड संस ने कोको पाउडर, चीनी और कोको बटर मिलाकर पहली ठोस चॉकलेट बार बनाई।

1875 में [[@switzerland|स्विट्ज़रलैंड]] के चॉकलेट बनाने वाले डेनियल पीटर ने उसमें गाढ़ा दूध मिलाया, जो उनके पड़ोसी हेनरी नेस्ले बनाते थे। इस तरह मिल्क चॉकलेट बनी। 1879 में रुडोल्फ़ लिंट ने कोंच नाम की मशीन बनाई, जो पिघली चॉकलेट को घंटों या दिनों तक चलाती रहती है। इससे चॉकलेट मुलायम हो जाती है और उसका स्वाद सधा हुआ। यह सब फ़ैक्टरी मशीनों के दौर, यानी [[@industrial-revolution|औद्योगिक क्रांति]], का हिस्सा था।

कोको बटर छह अलग-अलग आकार के [[crystal|क्रिस्टल]] में जम सकता है। इनमें से बस एक चॉकलेट को चमक और करारी "कट" वाली टूट देता है। इसलिए फ़ैक्टरियाँ चॉकलेट को गर्म करती हैं, ठंडा करती हैं और फिर हल्का-सा गुनगुना करती हैं, ताकि सही क्रिस्टल बनें। इसी को टेम्परिंग कहते हैं।

अगर कोई बार ज़्यादा गर्म होकर फिर ठंडी हो जाए, तो ग़लत क्रिस्टल बन जाते हैं और ऊपर सफ़ेद धारियाँ उभर आती हैं। इसे ब्लूम कहते हैं। देखने में अजीब लगता है, पर खाने में कोई ख़तरा नहीं।

कोको भारत में भी उगता है, मुख्य रूप से [[@kerala|केरल]], कर्नाटक, आंध्र प्रदेश और तमिलनाडु में, अक्सर [[@coconut|नारियल]] और सुपारी के पेड़ों के बीच। दुनिया के कोको में भारत का हिस्सा छोटा है, पर यहाँ चॉकलेट की बिक्री तेज़ी से बढ़ी है।

पश्चिमी अफ़्रीका के बहुत-से कोको किसान बहुत कम कमाते हैं। शोधकर्ताओं और समाजसेवी संस्थाओं ने पाया है कि वहाँ बहुत-से बच्चे स्कूल जाने के बजाय कोको के खेतों पर काम करते हैं। कुछ तो बड़े छुरों या रसायनों के साथ ख़तरनाक काम करते हैं। चॉकलेट कंपनियों और सरकारों ने इसे ख़त्म करने का वादा किया है, पर बदलाव धीमा रहा है।

text: केले अपने उगने के ढंग की वजह से टेढ़े होते हैं। वे बड़े-बड़े गुच्छों में एक डंडी पर उगते हैं, जो पौधे के ऊपर से नीचे लटकती है। शुरू में हर नन्हा केला ज़मीन की ओर इशारा करता है। बढ़ने के साथ वह धूप की ओर ऊपर मुड़ने लगता है।

वैज्ञानिक इस तरह बढ़ने को ऋणात्मक गुरुत्वानुवर्तन (नेगेटिव जियोट्रॉपिज़्म) कहते हैं, यानी [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] के खिंचाव से उलटी दिशा में बढ़ना। पौधों के तने हमेशा यही करते हैं। केले का फल पहले से नीचे की ओर मुँह किए होता है, इसलिए जब वह ऊपर मुड़ता है, तो मुस्कान जैसा आकार बन जाता है। घने [[rainforest|वर्षावनों]] में, जहाँ केले सबसे पहले जंगली रूप में उगे, रोशनी तक पहुँचना पौधे के जीने के लिए ज़रूरी था।

sec.t:
केले का पौधा मुंबई की दो-मंज़िला बस से भी ऊँचा हो सकता है, फिर भी वह पेड़ नहीं है। उसमें लकड़ी है ही नहीं। जो तना दिखता है, वह असल में "छद्म तना" है, जो विशाल पत्तों के निचले हिस्सों से बना है। ये हिस्से एक-दूसरे पर ऐसे कसकर लिपटे होते हैं जैसे लपेटा हुआ अख़बार।

एक बार फूल और फल देने के बाद वह तना मर जाता है। ज़मीन के नीचे वाले हिस्से से एक नया अंकुर, जिसे सकर कहते हैं, निकलता है और उसकी जगह ले लेता है। इस तरह केले का एक खेत कई सालों तक चलता रह सकता है।

वनस्पति वैज्ञानिक केले को बेरी कहते हैं, क्योंकि यह एक ही फूल से बनता है और इसके अंदर बीज होते हैं। अजीब बात है कि स्ट्रॉबेरी असली बेरी नहीं है। जंगली केले काली मिर्च जितने बड़े, सख़्त काले बीजों से भरे होते हैं, और उनमें गूदा मुश्किल से होता है।

हम जो केले खाते हैं, उन्हें हज़ारों सालों में ऐसा तैयार किया गया है कि उनके बीज नन्हे और नरम हों और उग न सकें। बीच के काले-काले धब्बे उन्हीं बीजों की निशानी हैं। इसलिए केले बीज से नहीं उगाए जा सकते। किसान सकर से, या प्रयोगशाला में उगाए गए [[tissue|ऊतक]] से नए पौधे तैयार करते हैं। एक तरह से, दुकान में रखा हर कैवेंडिश केला एक ही पौधे की नक़ल है।

भारत दुनिया के किसी भी देश से ज़्यादा [[@bananas|केले]] उगाता है, 2022 में दुनिया के कुल केलों का लगभग एक-चौथाई। ज़्यादातर केले भारत में ही रहते हैं: नाश्ते में खाए जाते हैं, सब्ज़ी में पकते हैं, या केरल में तलकर चिप्स बनते हैं। दक्षिण भारत की रसोई में कच्चा केला, केले का फूल, यहाँ तक कि तने का अंदरूनी हिस्सा भी पकाया जाता है।

यहाँ सैकड़ों किस्में हैं, नन्हे मीठे इलायची केलों से लेकर लाल केलों और केरल के बड़े नेंद्रन तक। [[@south-indian-meals|दक्षिण भारतीय भोजन]] अक्सर ताज़े केले के पत्ते पर परोसा जाता है, जो बड़ा होता है, पानी नहीं सोखता, और खाने के बाद फेंक दिया जाता है। बर्तन धोने का झंझट ही नहीं।

अमेरिका समेत दुनिया भर में बिकने वाले ज़्यादातर केले एक ही किस्म के हैं: कैवेंडिश। 1950 के दशक से पहले सबसे पसंदीदा किस्म ग्रो मिशेल थी। पनामा रोग नाम की एक [[fungus|फफूँद]] ने ग्रो मिशेल के बहुत-से खेत तबाह कर दिए, और किसान कैवेंडिश की ओर मुड़ गए।

अब उसी रोग का एक नया रूप एशिया, अफ़्रीका और लैटिन अमेरिका में कैवेंडिश पौधों पर हमला कर रहा है। क्योंकि हर कैवेंडिश एक ही पौधे की नक़ल है, उनमें से कोई भी इससे लड़ नहीं पाता। वैज्ञानिक ऐसे केले तैयार करने की होड़ में हैं जो इस रोग से बच सकें।

केलों का एक और अजीब राज़ है। उनमें पोटैशियम होता है, और उस पोटैशियम का एक बेहद छोटा हिस्सा कुदरती तौर पर [[radioactive|रेडियोधर्मी]] होता है। यह इतना कम है कि तुम्हें कोई नुकसान नहीं पहुँचा सकता, पर वैज्ञानिकों ने इस पर मज़ाक़ में एक इकाई तक बना डाली: "बनाना इक्विवेलेंट डोज़", यानी एक केले जितनी ख़ुराक।
